# Education in New Zealand
Education in New Zealand originated from Māori traditional knowledge transmission through wānanga (learning institutions run by elders) and was later formalized by European missionaries in the early 19th century. A national state education system, free, compulsory, and secular, was established in 1878, modeled largely on the Canterbury provincial system. Early childhood education is common and includes centre-based services such as Kindergartens ("kindy"), Puna Reo, and licensed daycare, with a requirement for qualified teachers and government licensure. Home-based and parent-led options like Kohanga Reo and Playcentre also exist, with licensed services following the national curriculum framework, Te Whāriki.
Primary and secondary schooling cover Years 1–13, starting typically at age 5 and continuing to about age 17, with compulsory education between ages 6 and 16. The structure includes eight years of primary education (Years 1–8), with Years 7 and 8 often designated as intermediate. Secondary education covers Years 9–13. The curriculum for state and state-integrated schools follows the New Zealand Curriculum (NZC) or Te Marautanga o Aotearoa (TMoA) for Māori-medium schools, emphasizing eight learning areas including languages, mathematics, arts, and sciences. Qualifications at senior levels include the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA), alongside options such as Cambridge International Examinations or International Baccalaureate. Schools are categorized as state (fully government funded), state-integrated (former private schools retaining special character, chiefly religious, charging attendance fees), and private (tuition-based, with fewer than 5% attendance). Home schooling is allowed under strict conditions demonstrating comparable education standards. Māori language education has seen revitalization efforts with Māori-medium and immersion schools operating under legal frameworks supporting the language, although enrollment trends have fluctuated.
Tertiary education encompasses a range of post-school education from informal community courses to undergraduate and advanced research degrees, regulated within the New Zealand Qualifications Framework. Funding includes government subsidies adjusted for socio-economic factors and voluntary parental donations. Special needs students receive additional support through targeted funding. Student loans and allowances assist with tertiary study costs. Despite efforts to improve educational outcomes, international assessments have highlighted challenges in mathematics and literacy, with particular attention to raising achievement levels for Māori and Pacific Island students. School bullying remains a concern with governmental initiatives in place but ongoing calls for comprehensive policies.
